## Regression

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(sf)
library(tidyverse)
library(tmap)
```

**Overview:**
This lab focuses on regression techniques. You'll be analyzing the association of various land cover, vegetation, climate, and terrain characteristics with summer land surface temperature (LST) in block groups across California, Oregon, and Washington. The goal is to understand which characteristics of places are associated with urban heat, and how well a linear regression model can explain it.

###Data and research questions###

Let's import the dataset.

```{r}
lab6_data<-st_read("data/lab6_gee_lstdata.gpkg") 
```

The variables in the dataset are:

* GISJOIN: Unique block group identifier from NHGIS (2020 block groups)
* lst_c: Land surface temperature (C), the median of clear-sky Landsat 8/9 observations from June-August 2021. This is the thermal "skin" temperature of the surface at the satellite overpass (late morning), not air temperature.
* ndvi: Normalized difference vegetation index from Landsat (June-August 2021 median). Values range from -1 to 1, with higher values indicating more vegetation.
* ndbi: Normalized difference built-up index from Landsat (June-August 2021 median). Higher values indicate more built-up or bare surfaces.
* ndwi: Normalized difference water index from Landsat (June-August 2021 median). Higher values indicate more water or moisture.
* impervious_pct: Percent of the 30 m pixel covered by impervious surface (data from the 2021 National Land Cover Database)
* tree_cover_pct: Percent tree canopy cover (data from MODIS Vegetation Continuous Fields, 250 m resolution)
* prism_tmean_c: Mean air temperature (C) from June-August 2021 (data from PRISM, 4 km resolution)
* prism_ppt_mm: Total precipitation (mm) from June-August 2021 (data from PRISM, 4 km resolution)
* elevation: Elevation in meters (data from the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission/NASA)
* slope: Terrain slope and aspect in degrees, derived from the elevation data
* nlcd_class/nlcd_label: Land cover class code and label (data from the 2021 National Land Cover Database)
* developed: 1 if the land cover class at the centroid is one of the NLCD developed classes (21-24), 0 otherwise

Our primary research question is how the vegetation, land cover, climate, and terrain variables in our dataset are predictive of land surface temperature. Note that the variables come from different sources at different spatial resolutions, and that the sample is dominated by developed areas (a large majority of block groups are in developed land cover classes), so our results speak most directly to urban and suburban heat.
